checks.diagnosis: The prompt lets cuts sever subject NPs from their finite verb, producing left fragments that the continuation must rescue.
checks.evidence: en_us_633, en_us_378, en_us_509, en_us_9 — each keeps a cut that leaves a noun/pronoun or named subject alone on the left while the main finite verb or predicate appears only on the right.
checks.type_predicate: a marker immediately follows a subject noun or pronoun (a full NP or name) and the next word to the right is a finite verb or auxiliary (e.g. is/are/was/blocked/observed/received).

edit.text: Do not cut between a subject noun/pronoun (or a full NP/name) and the sentence's following finite verb; keep subject and finite verb in the same piece.

orders.diagnosis: When two candidate cuts lie in the pre-verbal span, the prompt prefers later splits that leave left-side fragments; the better choice is the earlier split if it yields a grammatically complete clause on the left.
orders.evidence: en_us_9, en_us_633, en_us_381 — in each sentence two pre-verbal cuts compete and the measured target prefers the cut that yields a complete subject+verb span (earlier) over a later cut that leaves a fragment.
orders.type_predicate: two candidate markers both occur before the sentence's first finite verb (i.e. inside the same pre-verbal/initial constituent) so that one cut would leave a complete subject+verb on the left and the other would leave a fragment.

edit.text: When two cuts fall before the same finite verb, prefer the earlier cut if that earlier cut leaves the left span a grammatically complete clause (subject + finite verb) over the later cut that leaves a fragment.
